speaker: Barista
en_gloss: Hi there. Can I help you with your order?
learner_note_en: 도와드릴까요 = 'shall I help you?' — humble offering form. Standard service greeting in any Korean shop.

speaker: Visitor
ko_text: 네, 아이스 아메리카노 한 잔 주세요.
romanization: ne, aiseu amerikano han jan juseyo.
learner_note_en: 한 잔 = 'one cup'. 한 is the native Korean counter prefix; 잔 is the counter for cups/glasses. -주세요 = 'please give me'.

speaker: Barista
en_gloss: How would you like the size?
learner_note_en: Note 는 marking 사이즈 — 'as for the size'. 어떻게 = 'how'. The barista is asking which size to make for you.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 로 = 'in/with/as' — marks the form you want. Korean cafes use the same Tall/Grande/Venti words as Starbucks worldwide.

speaker: Barista
en_gloss: Will you be paying by card?
learner_note_en: 하시겠어요 = honorific 시 + future-intent 겠 + polite 어요. Service Korean stacks politeness markers like this constantly.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 할게요 = 'I'll do it' — declaring your own intent. Common pattern when committing to an action.

speaker: Barista
en_gloss: I'll give you a buzzer. Please wait just a moment.
learner_note_en: 진동벨 (vibration bell) = the puck-shaped pager that buzzes when your drink is ready. 잠시만 = 'just a moment'.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 감사합니다 is the formal 'thank you'. Use this with strangers, staff, elders. The casual version is 고마워요 / 고마워.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: Hello. Please go to this address.
learner_note_en: 주소로 = 'to the address' — 로 marks destination. 가주세요 = literally 'please go-give-me' (do this favor for me).

speaker: Driver
learner_note_en: -네요 ending = mild discovery, 'oh, I see'. Common when reacting to new information.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: Yes, that's right. How long does it take?
learner_note_en: 맞아요 = 'that's right' — useful confirming phrase. 얼마나 = 'how much / how long'.

speaker: Driver
learner_note_en: 정도 = 'about / approximately'. Korean Sino-Korean numbers used for minutes: 이십분 = 20 minutes.

speaker: Driver
learner_note_en: 다 왔어요 = 'we've arrived' (literally 'all came'). 만 = 10,000; 이천 = 2,000. 입니다 is the formal copula 'it is'.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: Tagging a noun with -요 turns it into a polite phrase: '카드요' = 'card, please / here's the card'.

speaker: Driver
learner_note_en: 되세요 = 'become / be (honorific)'. Set phrase: 좋은 ~ 되세요 = 'have a good ~'.

speaker: Clerk
en_gloss: Hi. Do you need a bag?
learner_note_en: 필요하세요 = 'do you need ~?' — honorific 시 inserted. Standard checkout question in Korea.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 하나 = 'one' (native Korean number used with counters or for standalone counting).

speaker: Clerk
learner_note_en: 백 = 100. -이에요 is the casual copula 'is'. Korean bag fees are usually 50–200 won.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 괜찮아요 is a Swiss-army phrase: 'it's OK / I'm fine / no problem / no thank you'. Tone and context decide which.

speaker: Clerk
learner_note_en: 다 해서 = 'all together'. 만 삼천 = 10,000 + 3,000 = 13,000.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: Same pattern as cafe scene — 로 marks 'by / with', 할게요 = 'I'll do it'.

speaker: Friend
ko_text: 민준아, 이쪽은 내 친구 존이야. 미국에서 왔어.
romanization: Minjun-a, ijjogeun nae chingu Jon-iya. Migukeseo wasseo.
en_gloss: Minjun, this is my friend John. He's from the US.
learner_note_en: 이쪽 = 'this side / this person' — the standard introduction frame. -아 after a name is a casual vocative used among friends.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: Hello. It's nice to meet you.
learner_note_en: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the formal first-meeting phrase. -겠습니다 sounds polished and respectful — common when meeting someone's family or a senior.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: -(이)라고 합니다 = 'I am called ~'. The polite formal self-introduction frame.

speaker: Minjun
en_gloss: Pleased to meet you. Where are you from?
learner_note_en: 반갑습니다 is more formal than 반가워요. 어디서 = 'from where'. 오셨어요 = honorific past polite of 오다 (to come).

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: I'm from the US. From Chicago.
learner_note_en: 에서 marks origin/source. Tagging a noun with -요 turns a one-word answer into a polite phrase.

speaker: Minjun
en_gloss: How long have you been in Korea?
learner_note_en: 엔 = 에 + 는 (location topic, contracted). 계시다 is the honorific form of 있다 ('to be / stay').

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: Two months. Please be good to me.
learner_note_en: 잘 부탁드립니다 (literally 'I humbly ask for your favor') is a set closing phrase when starting a relationship — work, study, friendship.

speaker: Friend
ko_text: 여기 비빔밥이 진짜 유명해. 한번 먹어봐.
romanization: yeogi bibimbap-i jinjja yumyeonghae. hanbeon meogeobwa.
en_gloss: The bibimbap here is really famous. Try it once.
learner_note_en: 한번 -아/어 봐 = 'try ~ once'. Casual register because they're friends — note no -요.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 그럼 = 'then / in that case'. -ㄹ게 is the casual version of -ㄹ게요 (committed intent).

speaker: Server
en_gloss: Welcome. Would you like to order?
learner_note_en: 어서 오세요 is the universal Korean welcome to a guest. Servers, shopkeepers, hosts all use it.

speaker: Friend
ko_text: 비빔밥 두 개랑 김치찌개 하나 주세요.
romanization: bibimbap du gae-rang kimchijjigae hana juseyo.
en_gloss: Two bibimbap and one kimchi stew, please.
learner_note_en: Counters: 두 개 = 'two (general items)', 하나 = 'one' (used standalone). -랑 = casual 'and / with'.

speaker: Server
learner_note_en: 매운 거 = 'spicy thing'. Korean restaurants commonly check spice tolerance with foreigners.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 건 = 거 + 는 (contracted). The whole noun phrase '매운 것' is the topic of comment.

speaker: Server
en_gloss: What would you like to drink?
learner_note_en: Same 'how shall I do?' frame as the cafe scenario — 어떻게 하시겠어요 covers many service questions.

speaker: Friend
en_gloss: Two glasses of water is fine. Thank you.
learner_note_en: -이면 돼요 = '~ is enough / that's all I need'. Useful for politely declining upsells.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: Excuse me. How do I get to Gangnam Station?
learner_note_en: 저, 죄송한데요 is the standard polite opener for stopping a stranger. 어떻게 가요 = 'how do you go'.

speaker: Local
learner_note_en: 2호선 = 'Line 2'. -시면 돼요 = '~ then it's fine' — extremely common in directions and instructions.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: Do I have to transfer here?
learner_note_en: 갈아타다 = 'to transfer (between trains/buses)'. -아야 돼요 = 'have to ~' (obligation).

speaker: Local
en_gloss: Yes, transfer at the next station.
learner_note_en: 다음 역 = 'next station'. -세요 attached to a verb is a polite directive — softer than a command.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: Same phrase you saw in the taxi scenario — works for any duration question.

speaker: Local
learner_note_en: 한 (before a number) = 'about'. 쯤 attached to a number/time = 'approximately'. Use either or both.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: Excuse me, how much are these apples?
learner_note_en: 사장님 = 'boss / owner' (honorific 님). The standard way to address shopkeepers and stall vendors.

speaker: Vendor
learner_note_en: 한 봉지 = 'one bag'. -에 (distributive) gives the 'per/each' meaning: 한 봉지에 = 'per bag'.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: That's a bit pricey — can you give me a discount?
learner_note_en: 깎다 literally means 'to shave / cut'. 깎아 주세요 = 'please cut (the price) for me' — the standard haggling request.

speaker: Vendor
ko_text: 에이, 안 돼요. 두 봉지 사시면 천 원 빼 드릴게요.
romanization: ei, an dwaeyo. du bongji sasimyeon cheon won ppae deurilgeyo.
en_gloss: Aw no, can't do that. Buy two bags and I'll knock off 1,000 won.
learner_note_en: 에이 is a soft refusal interjection. 사시면 = honorific conditional ('if you buy'). 빼 드릴게요 = humble 'I'll subtract for you'.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 그럼 = 'then / in that case'. Accepts the vendor's compromise.

speaker: Vendor
learner_note_en: 맛있게 드세요 (literally 'eat deliciously') is the universal Korean food farewell — vendors, hosts, parents all use it.

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: Formal thank-you, used to close any transaction.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: Hi. I think I've caught a cold.
learner_note_en: 감기에 걸리다 = 'to catch a cold'. -ㄴ/은 거 같아요 = 'it seems like ~' — useful for hedging.

speaker: Pharmacist
learner_note_en: 어떤 = 'what kind of'. 증상 = 'symptoms'. 있으세요 = honorific 'do you have'.

speaker: Visitor
en_gloss: I'm coughing and my throat hurts.
learner_note_en: 기침 = 'cough'. -하고 connects clauses: 'cough + and'. 목이 아파요 = 'throat hurts'.

speaker: Pharmacist
ko_text: 이 약 드시면 좀 나아지실 거예요.
romanization: i yak deusimyeon jom naajisil geoyeyo.
en_gloss: Take this medicine and you should feel better.
learner_note_en: 드시다 = honorific of 먹다. 나아지다 = 'to get better'. -ㄹ 거예요 = future ('will ~').

speaker: Visitor
learner_note_en: 하루에 = 'per day' (distributive 에). 몇 번 = 'how many times'.

speaker: Pharmacist
learner_note_en: 식후 = 'after meals' (식 'meal' + 후 'after' — Sino-Korean). 세 번 = 'three times'. 드세요 = polite honorific 'take/eat'.
